read.sections.0.heading.source: A vote, a transition and restored independence
read.sections.0.heading.back: A vote, a transition and restored independence

read.sections.0.text.source: Timor-Leste, also called East Timor, is on the island of Timor. Portugal ruled it for a long time. From the 1970s, Indonesia controlled it. On 30 August 1999, East Timorese voters took part in a vote run by the United Nations. Most voted to begin a move towards independence. After the vote there was violence, and many people had to leave their homes. A transition followed. A United Nations team ran the country, working with East Timorese leaders. On 20 May 2002, Timor-Leste's independence was restored. It had first declared independence in 1975. A country can celebrate on one day, but making schools work for every child takes much longer.
read.sections.0.text.back: Timor-Leste, which is also called East Timor, is on the island of Timor. Portugal ruled it for a long time. From the 1970s, Indonesia controlled it. On 30 August 1999, East Timorese voters took part in a vote run by the United Nations (UN). Most of them voted to begin a move towards independence. After the vote there was violence, and many people had to leave their homes. A transition period followed. A UN team ran the country, working with East Timorese leaders. On 20 May 2002, Timor-Leste's independence was restored. The country had first declared independence in 1975. A country can celebrate something in one day, but making schools work for every child takes much longer.

read.sections.0.simpler.source: Timor-Leste is also called East Timor. Portugal ruled it for a long time. Later, Indonesia controlled it. In 1999, people there voted. Most chose to move towards independence. After the vote there was violence. Many people had to leave their homes. Then came a transition. A United Nations team helped run the country. On 20 May 2002, independence was restored. A country can celebrate in one day. But good schools for every child take much longer.
read.sections.0.simpler.back: Timor-Leste is also called East Timor. Portugal ruled that country for a long time. Later, Indonesia controlled it. In 1999, the people there voted. Most of them chose to move towards independence. After the vote there was violence. Many people had to leave their homes. Then came a transition period. A UN team helped run the country. On 20 May 2002, independence was restored. A country can celebrate something in one day. But good schools for every child take much longer.

read.sections.1.text.source: Rebuilding schools began during the transition, not after it. In March 2000, a United Nations report said most children who had been in primary school were back in class. Many schools had been repaired, often with new roofs. In some places, teachers, parents and communities helped restart their schools. There was no standard curriculum yet. Teachers taught in Tetum, Indonesian, Portuguese or English. In 2004, a researcher called Susan Nicolai wrote a study for UNESCO. She found that rebuilding focused mostly on buildings, and less on plans for teachers, books and language. Her study looks back at events. It is not a diary written by a child in 1999.
read.sections.1.text.back: Rebuilding of schools began during the transition period, not after it. In March 2000, a UN report stated that most children who had been in primary school were back in class. Many schools had been repaired, often with new roofs. In some places, teachers, parents and communities helped restart their schools. There was no standard curriculum yet. Teachers taught in Tetum, Indonesian, Portuguese or English. In 2004, a researcher named Susan Nicolai wrote a study for UNESCO. She found that rebuilding focused mostly on buildings, and less on plans for teachers, books and language. Her study looks back at events that had happened. That study is not a diary written by a child in 1999.

read.sections.1.simpler.source: Work on schools started during the transition. It did not wait until 2002. In March 2000, a UN report said most children were back in class. Many schools got new roofs. Teachers, parents and communities helped. There was no curriculum for all schools yet. Teachers used four different languages. In 2004, Susan Nicolai wrote a study about this time. She found that people fixed buildings first. Plans for teachers, books and languages came more slowly.
read.sections.1.simpler.back: Work on repairing schools began during the transition period. That work did not wait until 2002. In March 2000, a UN report stated most children were back in class. Many schools got new roofs. Teachers, parents and communities helped. There was no curriculum for all schools yet. Teachers used four different languages. In 2004, Susan Nicolai wrote a study about this time. She found people repaired buildings first. Plans for teachers, books and languages came more slowly.

read.sections.2.text.source: The Government of Timor-Leste lists Tetum and Portuguese as the official languages. People also speak many other local languages. UNICEF, the United Nations' agency for children, says the country has rebuilt its schools since 2002, and more children now go to school. It also names problems: old buildings, many languages, and fewer school facilities in country areas. UNICEF works with the government on school repairs, teaching and schools where students and parents take part. The photo shows one school in 2024. It cannot tell us if students there have books or trained teachers. It cannot show if they have access to lessons in a language they know.
read.sections.2.text.back: The Government of Timor-Leste lists Tetum and Portuguese as the official languages. Its people also speak many other local languages. UNICEF, the UN's agency for children, states that the country has rebuilt its schools since 2002, and now more children go to school. UNICEF also names some problems: old buildings, many languages, and fewer school facilities in rural areas. UNICEF works with the government on repairing schools, teaching, and schools that involve pupils and parents. The photo shows one school in 2024. The photo cannot tell us whether pupils there have books or trained teachers. The photo cannot show whether they have access to lessons in a language they understand.

watch.summary.source: This UNICEF report was made in 2011. It visits a primary school in Laclubar, a town in the mountains of Timor-Leste. After the vote in 1999, many people left their homes. The school was left with no roof, desks or chairs. When people came back, local school leaders asked teachers to return. Parents gave chairs, tables and other things the school needed. The minister of education says the country had to start its schools again from the beginning. The government worked with UNICEF to plan new lessons, fix schools and train teachers. Now the school uses a child-friendly way of teaching. Students and parents take part in school life.
watch.summary.back: This UNICEF report was made in 2011. This report visits a primary school in Laclubar, a town in the mountain area of Timor-Leste. After the vote in 1999, many people left their homes. The school was left without a roof, desks or chairs. When people returned, local school leaders asked teachers to come back. Parents gave chairs, tables and other things the school needed. The minister of education said the country had to start its schools again from the beginning. The government worked with UNICEF to plan new lessons, repair schools and train teachers. Now the school uses a child-friendly way of teaching. Pupils and parents take part in school life.

educatorNotes.0.source: Aim: learners choose two priorities for rebuilding education, give a source-based reason for each, and name a trade-off. Evidence move: ask what a school needs besides walls. A sound answer gives two priorities supported by the UN report, the IIEP study or UNICEF, and a reasonable trade-off. Misconceptions to address: "independence instantly solved education", "education work only started after 2002", and "all learners speak both official languages".
educatorNotes.0.back: Aim: learners choose two priorities for rebuilding education, give a source-based reason for each one, and name one trade-off. Evidence step: ask what a school needs besides walls. A good answer gives two priorities supported by the UN report, the IIEP study or UNICEF, and one reasonable trade-off. Misconceptions to address: "independence immediately solved the problems of education", "education work only started after 2002", and "all learners speak both official languages".

educatorNotes.1.source: Languages: the Government of Timor-Leste lists Portuguese and Tetum (Tétum, the national language) as official, English and Indonesian as working languages, and about 15 other local languages. Talk about this without deficit framing: many languages are a strength and a planning question, not a problem in children. Source caveats: UNICEF's page gives percentages with no date, so the lesson does not use them as current rates. The IIEP abstract dates the consultation to September 1999 (the vote was on 30 August; the result came in September). The UN news item shows only "23 March"; its address and content (UNTAET, the earlier international force) place it in 2000.
educatorNotes.1.back: Languages: the Government of Timor-Leste lists Portuguese and Tetum (Tétum, the national language) as official languages, English and Indonesian as working languages, and about 15 other local languages. Discuss this without treating it as a weakness: many languages are a strength and a planning question, not a problem in children. Source caveats: UNICEF's page gives percentages with no date, so this lesson does not use them as current rates. The IIEP abstract gives the date of the popular vote as September 1999 (the vote took place on 30 August; its result came out in September). The UN news item shows only "23 March"; its address and content (UNTAET, the earlier international force) place it in 2000.
educatorNotes.1.note: "deficit framing" rendered as "menganggapnya sebagai kelemahan" (treating it as a weakness). "consultation" (the 1999 popular consultation) rendered "pungutan suara" (popular vote).
